questions.text: Why can a decompiler recover a stored parameter name while inventing a local name from the same .NET assembly?

options.A: Every name is stored directly in the CIL instruction bytes.
options.B: Param metadata can retain parameter names, while local names may require an absent PDB.
options.C: The runtime renames every local variable to match its parameter.
options.D: A decompiler can always reconstruct all original names from their types.

questions.explanation: The Param table carries parameter names. Local signatures carry local types, while original local names require debug information such as a PDB.

questions.text: A Python decompiler reports Unsupported opcode on a pyc you compiled yourself. What should you check before concluding the file is obfuscated?

options.A: Whether renaming the file changes its bytecode instructions.
options.B: Whether the source filename is an absolute filesystem path.
options.C: Whether the file contains more constants than local variables.
options.D: The pyc magic word and the decompiler’s supported bytecode versions.

questions.explanation: The header identifies the producer version. An older opcode table can reject valid newer bytecode, so a version mismatch must be checked first.

questions.text: The JVM reader computes a branch target as start + signed_displacement, where start is the branch opcode’s address. For start=30 and displacement=-20, what target does it produce?
questions.explanation: JVM branch offsets are relative to the opcode address: 30 + (-20) = 10, without adding the instruction length.
